bai.ten: Black holes: where light cannot escape
bai.moTa: Fly around a black hole rendered from the actual paths of light, and compare it with EHT images
bai.yChinh: Compress a mass inside its **Schwarzschild radius** $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, and even light cannot escape. Each pixel in this view comes from a ray of light traced backward using Einstein’s equations. The shadow is 5.2 rs across, the far side of the gas disk is visible, and one side is brighter. The Event Horizon Telescope has imaged these features.
bai.giaiThich:
- Schwarzschild radius $r_s = 2GM/c^2$: Sun 2.95 km, Earth 8.9 mm, Sgr A* 12.7 million km, M87* 128 AU.
- The shadow consists of viewing directions in which a ray traced backward reaches the horizon. Its diameter $3\sqrt3\,r_s \approx 5{,}2\,r_s$ is much larger than the horizon.
- Light circling the photon sphere forms higher-order images that pile up into a photon ring along the edge of the shadow.
- The gas disk is flat, but light bending over and under the black hole reveals its far side. The Doppler effect makes one side brighter; redshift dims the inner edge.
- EHT: M87*’s ring measured 42 ± 3 microarcseconds across (2019), and Sgr A*’s about 52 microarcseconds (2022), consistent with shadow sizes calculated from their masses.
- The model uses a nonrotating black hole. Real black holes rotate (Kerr): the shadow is slightly offset, and the inner edge of the disk shifts inward or outward.
bai.conSo.1: **Sagittarius A***: 4.3 million solar masses, horizon radius 12.7 million km. The EHT released its image in 2022; the bright ring measures about 52 microarcseconds.
bai.conSo.2: **M87***: 6.5 billion solar masses, horizon radius 128 AU, more than 4 times Neptune’s orbital radius. The first image of a black hole was published on 4/10/2019; the bright ring measures 42 ± 3 microarcseconds.
bai.conSo.3: **5.2 rs** (exactly $3\sqrt3$): the shadow’s diameter as seen from far away.
bai.conSo.4: **A factor of 81**: the brightness contrast between opposite sides of the inner disk edge due to the Doppler effect.
bai.hieuDung: **A black hole is no vacuum cleaner.** At a distance, its gravity is exactly the same as that of a star of the same mass. If the Sun suddenly became a black hole of equal mass, Earth would stay in its present orbit, although the sky would turn dark and Earth would grow cold. The dark shadow in the image is wider than two and a half horizon diameters; it is not the hole’s “surface.”
bai.nguon: Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration 2019, ApJL 875, L1 (M87*: mass 6.5 billion M☉, distance 16.8 Mpc, ring 42 ± 3 µas), and 2022, ApJL 930, L12 (Sgr A*: ring 51.8 ± 2.3 µas). Sgr A* mass and distance: GRAVITY Collaboration. Mass of M87* from stellar motions: Gebhardt et al. 2011. Innermost circular orbit of a rotating black hole: Bardeen, Press and Teukolsky 1972. Constants: CODATA 2018, IAU 2012. The disk colors are illustrative; the actual gas is much hotter.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.1: Calculate an object’s Schwarzschild radius from its mass.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.2: Explain why the shadow is 5.2 rs across while the horizon diameter is 2 rs.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.3: Interpret a black hole image: the disk’s far side, the photon ring, the brighter side, and the dark inner edge.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.4: Compare the shadow size calculated from mass and distance with actual EHT images.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.5: Describe how a computer renders the image by tracing light rays backward, and how rotation changes a black hole.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.noiDung:
You are hovering far from a black hole surrounded by a rotating disk of hot gas. A single number sets its size, the {{bán kính Schwarzschild|Schwarzschild radius}}:

$$ r_s = \frac{2GM}{c^2} $$

Here $M$ is mass, $G$ is the gravitational constant, and $c$ is the speed of light. Compress the mass $M$ inside this radius and nothing can escape, even light.

| Object | Mass | Schwarzschild radius |
|---|---|---|
| Earth | 0.000003 | 8.9 mm |
| Sun | 1 | 2.95 km |
| Stellar-mass black hole | 10 | 29.5 km |
| Sagittarius A* | 4.3 million | 12.7 million km (18 times the Sun’s radius) |
| M87* | 6.5 billion | 128 AU (more than 4 times Neptune’s orbital radius) |

Masses are in solar units. Measured in $r_s$, the image in the model **looks exactly the same** for every mass. Only the physical scale and the numbers in the data panel change.

> [Thử ngay] Choose the black hole for the data panel: [[Sgr A*|sgr]] [[M87*|m87]] [[10 solar masses|sao]]

> [Lịch sử] In 1783 John Michell, and later Laplace, considered a Newtonian “dark star” from which light could not escape. In early 1916, a few weeks after Einstein published his field equations, Karl Schwarzschild found an exact solution for a spherical mass. John Wheeler popularized the term “black hole” in 1967.

+++ Go deeper: a coincidence with Newtonian escape speed
In Newtonian mechanics, the escape speed from a surface of radius $r$ is $v = \sqrt{2GM/r}$. Setting $v = c$ gives exactly $r = 2GM/c^2$.

For the Sun, $GM = 1{,}327\times10^{20}\ \text{m}^3/\text{s}^2$, so $r_s = 2\times1{,}327\times10^{20}/(2{,}998\times10^8)^2 \approx 2\,953$ m.

The physical meanings differ. At a Newtonian “dark star,” light would climb some distance and then fall back. At Einstein’s horizon, outward-directed light **stays at the horizon**, and inside it every future direction leads toward the center (Lesson 16). The formulas coincide because of the algebra and the choice of coordinate $r$, although the underlying pictures are different.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.ten: The event horizon: a one-way membrane
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.noiDung:
Switch off the gas disk, leaving the black hole against a background of stars. The {{Chân trời sự kiện|event horizon}} at $r = r_s$ is a boundary in spacetime. Like a one-way membrane, it can be crossed inward but never outward. There is no material surface there.

The data panel shows two things about **hovering at rest** here under rocket power:

- Your clock runs more slowly by the factor $\sqrt{1 - r_s/r}$ (Lesson 9). At 1.1 rs it runs at just 30.2% of the distant rate.
- It also shows the stretching across your body (tidal force, Lesson 12).

> [Con số] At the horizon, a person 2 m tall experiences a tidal stretch of about **21 million times** Earth’s gravity for a black hole of 10 solar masses, but only about **1 part in 10,000** of Earth’s gravity at Sgr A*. The larger the hole, the gentler its horizon.

> [Thử ngay] Drag the blue dot, a stationary signal transmitter, to a spot near the black hole and release it. It falls freely inward. You see it slow down, redden, fade, and finally disappear just outside the horizon, although its own clock shows it crossing the horizon in a finite time. The data panel gives both accounts.
> [[Release the transmitter|tha]] [[Fly to the photon sphere|photon]] [[Fly close to the horizon|sat]] [[Return to the previous view|canh]]

> [Lưu ý] The transmitter’s sound and color are mapped to the range of hearing and vision. It emits an 880 Hz beep every 1 rs/c on its own clock and flashes blue light at 440 nm. You hear each beep at $g \times 880$ Hz and see the light at $440/g$ nm, where $g$ is the ratio of received to emitted frequency. This includes gravitational redshift and Doppler shift, calculated along the actual light ray from the transmitter to you. The beeps are spaced by the reception intervals on your clock, growing farther apart as their pitch drops. Time is compressed: 1 second of listening represents 5 rs/c on your clock (about 3.5 minutes for Sgr A*).

> [Lưu ý] Hovering near the horizon requires enormous thrust. The sky contracts into a small bright region overhead, and starlight shifts toward the blue and grows more intense. Lesson 16 explores the light cones at the horizon and inside it.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.thuThach.de: Drag the transmitter to a position from which it would reach the horizon in exactly **15 rs/c** on its own clock (within 0.75). Then release it into free fall.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.thuThach.goiY: Hover over the blue dot. Its tooltip gives the time to the horizon if you release it there. The farther out you start, the longer it falls. The target is about 4.6 rs from the center.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.noiDung:
The central dark region is the black hole’s **shadow**. The two circles that just appeared show how much larger it looks than the horizon:

- **Green circle**: the shadow edge calculated by the model.
- **Dashed red circle**: how large the horizon would look if light traveled in straight lines.

From here (15.7 rs), the shadow spans 18.4° of sky. The straight-line horizon would span only 7.3°.

The shadow consists of viewing directions in which light rays traced **backward** from your eye lead to the horizon. It is not a picture of the horizon’s surface. As we saw in Lesson 14, every ray with an impact parameter below $b_c = (3\sqrt3/2)\,r_s$ is captured. For a very distant observer, the shadow edge has radius $b_c$, so

$$ \text{đường kính bóng} = 2b_c = 3\sqrt3\,r_s \approx 5{,}2\,r_s $$

> [Thử ngay] [[Fly farther away|xa]] [[Return to 15.7 rs|canh]] [[Go to the photon sphere|photon]]
> At the photon sphere, the shadow fills exactly **half the sky** (180°). Scroll to fly inward or outward and drag to change your viewing angle. The data panel shows how many degrees the shadow spans.

+++ Go deeper: shadow size for an observer at distance $r$
A stationary observer at radius $r$ sees the shadow edge at an angle $\theta$ from the direction to the center, where

$$ \sin\theta = \frac{b_c}{r}\sqrt{1 - \frac{r_s}{r}} $$

The factor $\sqrt{1-r_s/r}$ converts the ray direction in Schwarzschild coordinates into the direction a stationary observer measures with local rulers and clocks. At $r = 15{,}7\,r_s$: $\sin\theta = 2{,}598/15{,}7\times\sqrt{0{,}936} = 0{,}160$, $\theta = 9{,}2°$, giving a shadow 18.4° wide. At $r = 1{,}5\,r_s$: $\sin\theta = 1{,}732\times0{,}577 = 1$, $\theta = 90°$. Far away: $\theta \approx b_c/r$.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.thuThach.de: Scroll to fly closer until the dark shadow spans **90°** of the sky, one quarter of the way around you (within 3°).
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.thuThach.goiY: Read “Shadow spans” in the data panel. The radius you are looking for is a familiar one: exactly the radius of the gas disk’s inner edge.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.ten: Lensing around a black hole: layers of images
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.noiDung:
The blue grid shows longitude and latitude **drawn on the distant sky**, like the lines on a globe. Without the black hole, its lines would be regular. Here the grid is distorted by an extreme example of the gravitational lensing from Lesson 14.

- The sky directly behind the black hole appears as an **Einstein ring** encircling the shadow.
- A background star has at least **two images**: one formed by light passing on one side of the hole, and another by light bending around the other side.
- In fact there are **infinitely many images**. A ray can travel an extra half turn, full turn, turn and a half, and so on around the photon sphere before reaching you. Each extra half turn narrows the image by a factor of about $e^\pi \approx 23$. These images accumulate in a thin band along the shadow edge: the {{vành photon|photon ring}}.

> [Thử ngay] [[Show sky grid|luoi]] [[Hide grid|tat]] [[Turn away and look out into the universe|ra]] [[Look toward the black hole|vao]]
> Hover over the sky. The tooltip tells you how many degrees the ray reaching that pixel has bent and how far the star’s actual position is from its apparent one. The stars and the Milky Way in the background show the real sky.

+++ Go deeper: why each layer narrows by a factor of $e^\pi$
Close to the critical impact parameter, the deflection angle grows logarithmically:

$$ \alpha(b) \approx -\ln\Big(\frac{b - b_c}{b_c}\Big) + \text{hằng số} $$

For an extra $\pi$ (half turn), $\ln(b - b_c)$ must decrease by $\pi$. The interval $b - b_c$ therefore narrows by a factor of $e^\pi \approx 23{,}1$. Numerical integration of the model’s own equation gives the same ratio. The coefficient of 1 in front of the logarithm is specific to a nonrotating black hole.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.thuThach.de: Hover close to the edge of the shadow. Find a spot in the sky where the arriving light has been bent **more than 180°**. It comes from a star almost behind you, loops around the far side of the black hole, and comes back.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.thuThach.goiY: The most strongly bent rays lie in a very thin ring just outside the shadow. Move outward from its edge a little at a time and read the angle in the tooltip.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.ten: The accretion disk: seeing its far side
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.noiDung:
Turn the gas disk back on and temporarily disable the Doppler effect to see its shape. The {{Đĩa bồi tụ|accretion disk}} in the model is **as flat as Saturn’s rings**. It extends from 3 rs (the innermost stable circular orbit, Lesson 13) to 12 rs. Yet the image looks like a hat:

- The **arc above the shadow** comes from the part of the disk **behind** the black hole. Light from its upper surface bends over the top of the hole to reach you.
- The **thin band below the shadow** is the underside of that same part of the disk. Its light bends underneath.
- The **thin bright ring beside the shadow edge** is a higher-order image. Its light traveled more than half a turn around the hole.

The part behind the black hole remains visible; bending makes it appear somewhere else.

> [Thử ngay] [[Look edge-on|ngang]] [[View from above|tren]] [[Classic view|canh]]
> Seen edge-on, the far side of the disk forms a full circle around the shadow. Viewed from above, the disk is almost undistorted, apart from the ring of higher-order images. Hover over the arc above the shadow: the tooltip identifies gas behind the hole and gives the angle its ray swept out around the center.

> [Lưu ý] For visibility the modeled disk is infinitely thin and ends at 12 rs. Its temperature colors are illustrative. The real gas is much hotter and also emits strongly at X-ray and radio wavelengths.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.ten: One side shines brighter: Doppler shift and redshift
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.noiDung:
Turn the Doppler effect back on. One side of the disk lights up and the other grows much dimmer. At the inner edge the gas orbits at **half the speed of light**. On the side moving toward us, its light is concentrated, brighter, and bluer. The opposite happens on the receding side.

Let $g$ be the ratio of the frequency we receive to the frequency the gas emits. At the inner edge (3 rs), for light emitted along the direction of rotation, compare the following cases:

| Side | Frequency ratio | Relative brightness |
|---|---|---|
| approaching gas | 1.41 | 4 |
| perpendicular emission | 0.71 | 0.25 |
| receding gas | 0.47 | 0.05 |

The two sides differ by a factor of **81**. The middle row shows that $g$ is below 1 even without the line-of-sight Doppler effect. The orbiting gas clock at 3 rs runs at 70.7% of the distant clock rate, so the light shows {{dịch chuyển đỏ hấp dẫn|gravitational redshift}}. This **dims the inner edge**, even though the gas is hottest at about 4.1 rs.

> [Thử ngay] [[Disable Doppler effect|tat]] [[Enable Doppler effect|bat]] [[Stop the disk|dung]] [[Rotate the disk|quay]]
> Hover over the disk to read $g$ at each point. With sound on, you also hear a tone at $440 \times g$ Hz (mapped to the audible range). Its pitch rises on the approaching side and falls on the receding side and close to the inner edge.

+++ Go deeper: the formula for $g$ and the fourth power
Consider gas in a circular orbit of radius $r$ (angular speed $\Omega = \sqrt{GM/r^3}$ by a distant clock) and a ray whose angular momentum divided by its energy is $\ell$:

$$ g = \frac{\sqrt{1 - \frac{3r_s}{2r}}}{1 - \Omega\ell/c} $$

The numerator is the gas clock rate on a circular orbit (Lesson 13); the denominator gives the Doppler effect. At 3 rs a tangentially emitted ray has $\Omega\ell/c = \pm0{,}5$, giving $g = 0{,}707/0{,}5 = 1{,}41$ or $0{,}707/1{,}5 = 0{,}47$.

Brightness is proportional to $g^4$. Each photon carries $g$ times the energy; photons arrive $g$ times more frequently; and the beam is concentrated into a solid angle smaller by a factor of $g^2$.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.thuThach.de: Leave the Doppler effect on. Hover over the disk to find a spot where the light reaches you **without a change in frequency**: $g = 1$ (within 0.02). There the Doppler effect exactly offsets gravitational redshift.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.thuThach.goiY: The approaching gas has g above 1; the receding gas and gas close to the inner edge have g below 1. Look for the boundary on the brighter half of the disk.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.ten: Real images: M87* in 2019 and Sgr A* in 2022
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.noiDung:
Look down on the black hole from about 17° off its rotation axis, as we do for M87*. A bright ring surrounds a dark region, and one side is brighter. This is what the **Event Horizon Telescope** (EHT) imaged.

The EHT links radio telescopes on several continents to form an Earth-sized telescope observing at a wavelength of 1.3 mm. Its resolution is of order the wavelength divided by Earth’s diameter, about **21 microarcseconds**: enough to see an orange on the Moon.

| | M87* | Sgr A* |
|---|---|---|
| Mass (solar masses) | 6.5 billion | 4.3 million |
| Distance | 16.8 Mpc | 26,700 light-years |
| Calculated shadow: $5{,}2\,r_s$ divided by distance | 39.7 µas | 54 µas |
| Measured bright ring | 42 ± 3 µas (published 4/10/2019) | 51.8 ± 2.3 µas (published 5/12/2022) |

The symbol µas means microarcseconds. The bright ring comes from gas just outside the shadow edge, so its size does not exactly match the shadow edge: depending on where the gas glows, the ring can be slightly larger or smaller than the shadow. The masses and distances also carry uncertainties of a few percent. The mass of 6.5 billion for M87* was itself derived by the EHT from the ring size, and it agrees with the mass measured from the motions of stars around it (about 6.6 billion). For Sgr A*, the mass and distance were measured independently from the orbit of the star S2, and the ring differs from the calculated shadow by only about 4%, within the uncertainties: the black-hole geometry of general relativity holds right up to the horizon.

> [Thử ngay] [[View as for M87*|tren]] [[Classic view|canh]] [[M87* data|m87]] [[Sgr A* data|sgr]]

> [Lưu ý] EHT images are blurred because the resolution is about half the ring diameter. The modeled image is sharp because the computer does not face that limit. The lower part of M87*’s ring is brighter. The EHT attributes this to orbiting gas and the Doppler effect from the previous step. In this nearly face-on view, the model smooths the gas texture and exaggerates the brightness difference between the two sides so it is easy to see (illustrative); the exact calculation makes the approaching side only about twice as bright as the other.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.8.ten: How the computer renders the image; what changes with spin
bai.baiGiang.buoc.8.noiDung:
The computer builds this image using {{dò tia ngược|backward ray tracing}}. It works **outward from the eye**, opposite to the light’s direction. For each pixel:

1. Take the viewing direction through the pixel and convert it to a direction in Schwarzschild coordinates.
2. Solve the light-path equation from Lesson 14 step by step, for up to 300 steps. Steps are small near the black hole and grow larger farther away.
3. Whenever the ray crosses the disk plane between 3 rs and 12 rs, add the gas color there, multiplied by $g^4$.
4. If the ray falls below $r_s$, the pixel is dark. If it escapes, take the sky color in its final direction.

A 1600 × 1000 screen has 1.6 million pixels, so one frame can require up to **480 million steps**. The graphics processor handles the rays in parallel. We work backward because only a tiny fraction of the rays emitted by the gas ever reach our eye.

> [Lưu ý] This model uses a **nonrotating** black hole. Nearly all real black holes rotate (the Kerr solution, 1963), dragging surrounding spacetime into rotation. The inner disk edge can move inward to **0.5 rs** for gas orbiting with the spin (releasing up to 42% of its rest mass as energy), or outward to **4.5 rs** for the opposite direction. The shadow **shifts to one side** and flattens slightly along one edge, but its size changes by only a few percent. This is why EHT images constrain mass better than spin.

> [Thử ngay] [[Fly close to the horizon|sat]] [[Turn away and look out into the universe|ra]] [[Return to the classic view|canh]]
> Hover over any pixel. The computer retraces that exact ray with the same algorithm, telling you whether it falls through the horizon, where it meets the disk, or which star it came from.

Lesson 16 draws the horizon’s causal structure with light cones and follows an object through it.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.2.y: The angular diameter equals $5{,}2\,r_s$ divided by distance.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.3.ten: Shadow size as seen from radius r
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.3.y: $\theta$ is the angular radius of the shadow; at 1.5 rs the shadow covers half the sky.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.4.y: Numerator: the gas clock runs slowly. Denominator: Doppler effect.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.hoi: If all of Earth were compressed into a black hole, about how large would its horizon radius be?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.giai: $r_s = 2GM/c^2$ with $GM_{\text{TĐ}} = 3{,}99\times10^{14}\ \text{m}^3/\text{s}^2$ gives $8{,}9\times10^{-3}$ m, about the size of a marble. The value 2.95 km is for the Sun.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.hoi: Why is the shadow about 5.2 rs across, rather than 2 rs (the horizon diameter)?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.chon.1: A layer of dark gas around the horizon blocks some light
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.chon.2: Every ray with an impact parameter below 2.6 rs bends inward and falls through the horizon
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.chon.4: Earth’s atmosphere acts as a lens and magnifies the image
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.giai: The shadow consists of directions in which tracing a ray backward leads to the horizon. The critical impact parameter is $b_c = (3\sqrt3/2)\,r_s \approx 2{,}6\,r_s$, giving a shadow diameter of $2b_c \approx 5{,}2\,r_s$.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.hoi: The gas disk is flat, and we see it almost edge-on. Why is there still a bright arc arching above the shadow?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.chon.1: The disk actually bends upward at the back
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.chon.2: Light from the disk behind the black hole bends over the top and reaches our eyes
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.chon.3: Gas at the back is hotter
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.chon.4: It is a jet emerging from the black hole
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.giai: The part behind the hole remains visible. Its light bends around the hole and appears above it (top surface of the disk) and below it (underside). The disk stays flat.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.hoi: Why is one side of the disk much brighter?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.1: It lies closer to the black hole
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.2: Gas there is moving toward us: the Doppler effect makes its light brighter and bluer
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.chon.4: The black hole sucks in light from the other side
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.giai: Gas at the inner edge orbits at about half the speed of light. Brightness is proportional to $g^4$: on the approaching side $g \approx 1{,}41$, on the receding side $g \approx 0{,}47$, giving a contrast of about a factor of 81.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.hoi: M87* has about 1,500 times the mass of Sgr A*, yet the two bright rings are nearly the same size in EHT images. Why?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.chon.1: The EHT enlarged the Sgr A* image for comparison
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.chon.2: M87* is about 2,000 times farther away, almost canceling the difference in angular size
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.chon.3: Shadow size is independent of mass
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.giai: The angular size of the shadow is $5{,}2\,r_s$ divided by distance, and $r_s$ is proportional to mass. With about 1,500 times the mass at about 2,000 times the distance (16.8 Mpc versus 8.2 kpc), M87* even looks slightly smaller: 40 versus 54 microarcseconds.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.6.hoi: Describe how the computer determines the color of one pixel in the black hole image.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.6.dap: The computer takes the viewing direction through that pixel and traces a ray backward from the eye by solving the null geodesic equation in small steps. Each time the ray crosses a gas-filled part of the disk plane, it adds the color of that gas, based on temperature and frequency-shift factor $g$, with brightness multiplied by $g^4$. If the ray dips below the Schwarzschild radius, the rest is black. If it escapes, the computer adds the sky color from its final direction. Tracing backward calculates only rays that actually reach the eye.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.1: Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration 2019, ApJL 875, L1: first image of the shadow of the black hole M87*.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.2: Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration 2022, ApJL 930, L12: the image of Sagittarius A*.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.3: J. B. Hartle, *Gravity: An Introduction to Einstein’s General Relativity* (2003), chapter 12: gravitational collapse and black holes.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.4: K. S. Thorne, *Black Holes and Time Warps* (1994): the history of the black hole idea, from “dark stars” to rotating black holes.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.1.nghia: The dark region of the sky comprising directions in which a light ray traced backward reaches the horizon. For a nonrotating black hole its diameter is $3\sqrt3\,r_s \approx 5{,}2\,r_s$.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.2.nghia: A narrow bright ring beside the shadow’s edge, made of images formed by light that has traveled half a turn, a full turn, or more around the photon sphere.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.3.nghia: A disk of gas spiraling toward a massive object. Friction heats it and makes it shine. Around a nonrotating black hole the inner edge lies at about 3 rs.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.4.nghia: An imaging method that traces each ray outward from the eye, opposite to the light’s actual direction, and determines what it meets.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.5.nghia: A rotating black hole (Roy Kerr’s solution, 1963). It drags surrounding spacetime into rotation. Its shadow is slightly offset and the inner disk edge shifts.
